summary: Specifies how to use DNS SRV records to find services for the AFS distributed file system, and how to read priority and weight values. It deprecates the AFSDB record from RFC 1183 for locating AFS database servers. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A shared file system uses a more modern address book entry to find its servers, and the old entry is retired.

questions: how to find afs cell servers with dns
what is an afs srv record
subtitle: How AFS clients find a cell's database servers with DNS SRV records instead of the old AFSDB record.

tldr.problem: AFS clients needed to find the VLDB and PTS servers of a cell, but the AFSDB record from RFC 1183 has no priority, no port or protocol, and assumes both services run on one host.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SRV labels for the two services, _afs3-vlserver and _afs3-prserver, and says how SRV priority and weight map to the preference ranks AFS clients already use.
tldr.outcome: AFSDB is deprecated for locating AFS cell database servers, though cells are still advised to publish AFSDB records for older clients. A later RFC updates this one.

today: RFC 5864 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1183 by deprecating AFSDB for locating AFS cell database servers, and it is itself updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: Why Move Beyond AFSDB
sections.content:
AFS is a distributed file system organized into cells. A cell has Volume Location Database (VLDB) servers, Protection Service (PTS) servers, and file and volume servers. A client first asks a VLDB server which file server holds a file's volume, then talks to that file server directly. It may also contact a PTS server to register or to query protection data.

So a client must find the VLDB and possibly PTS servers of a cell. Originally this was a per-client file called CellServDB, and RFC 1183 added the DNS AFSDB record for the job.

RFC 5864 lists the drawbacks of AFSDB: it has no priority or ranking, it carries no protocol or port information, it assumes VLDB and PTS run on the same host, and it is a little-known and little-supported corner of DNS. SRV records, defined in RFC 2782, fix all of these.
sections.plainLanguage: The old address-book entry could not say which server to call first or which door to use. The newer kind of entry can, so everyone switches to it.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
The document describes the format and use of SRV records for AFS service location, deprecates the AFSDB record for this purpose, and gives guidance for moving over and staying compatible with older clients.

It does not document the AFS protocol itself or the exact purpose of VLDB and PTS. AFSDB records are also used to locate servers for the OSF Distributed Computing Environment (DCE) naming system; that use is outside the scope and is left unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper only covers how to find the servers. How the shared folders work inside is someone else's story.

sections.title: SRV Record Names for AFS
sections.content:
An SRV record is named _<service>._<proto>.<name>. Two service values are defined: afs3-vlserver for VLDB servers and afs3-prserver for PTS servers. File and volume services are found by asking the VLDB, so they get no SRV records.

The proto part MUST be udp for the current AFS protocol, which uses Rx over UDP. Other values may be used if future AFS revisions support other protocols such as Rx over TCP.

The name MUST be the AFS cell name. Clients MUST query only for a name that exactly matches the cell of interest, and MUST NOT strip leading components to look for more general records. The cells prod.example.com and example.com are entirely different cells.

As with AFSDB, SRV records only work for cells whose names follow the structure of the DNS. Sites creating new cells SHOULD choose such names.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is labelled with which service it is for, which kind of connection to use, and the exact cell name. The cell name has to match exactly, like a full home address rather than just the street.

sections.title: Priority, Weight and Preference Ranks
sections.content:
As RFC 2782 requires, clients MUST try the reachable target with the lowest-numbered priority. Among targets of equal priority, the weight SHOULD feed a weighted selection, with larger weights proportionately more likely. A weight of 0 SHOULD be used when all targets at that priority are equal. Clients MAY also consider network performance, but such information MUST NOT override priority.

Many AFS implementations use preference ranks: each server gets a number when the client first contacts the cell, and the lowest rank is preferred until it goes down. Clients doing this SHOULD proceed in two steps. First, sort targets by priority and give each priority a base rank far enough apart from the others that no later adjustment can reorder them. The numeric value of a priority has no meaning, only the order. Second, within one priority, order targets with the RFC 2782 algorithm and increment the base rank so the first selected target has the lowest rank.

Clients MAY then adjust ranks dynamically, but only by amounts too small to move a server across a priority boundary. When the record's TTL expires, derived ranks MUST be discarded and regenerated, although accumulated metrics may be reused.

AFS ranks are conventionally 1 to 65535 and SRV priorities are 0 to 65535. If there are more distinct priorities than can be represented, clients SHOULD fall back to ranks based only on priorities. Implementations MUST be able to assign distinct base ranks for at least ten distinct priority values.
sections.plainLanguage: Priority is like a list of who to call first, second and third. Weight is like rolling a loaded die to share the calls among people on the same step. The client may peek at which servers are fast, but it never skips a higher step.

sections.title: Staying Compatible with AFSDB
sections.content:
Many clients support AFSDB but not SRV, so a cell that publishes SRV records SHOULD also publish AFSDB records. AFSDB cannot express priority, weight or port, so all listed servers are treated as equal. The AFSDB record SHOULD list servers that provide both VLDB and PTS on the standard ports (7003 and 7002) over Rx on UDP, and that either have the lowest-numbered priority or that the administrator is happy to have clients use first.

Administrators MAY use different server lists in the two record types. A cell SHOULD keep at least one VLDB and one PTS server on the standard ports, since clients without SRV support cannot find servers on other ports.

Clients SHOULD query SRV by default and then SHOULD fall back to AFSDB if no SRV records exist. An AFSDB record of subtype 1 SHOULD be treated as the equivalent pair of SRV records with priority 0, weight 0, and ports 7003 and 7002.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old phones cannot read the new address book, so you keep a short copy of the old kind of entry too. New phones look at the new one first and only use the old one if the new one is missing.

sections.title: A Worked Zone File
sections.content:
The RFC gives a fictional example.com zone that shows the range of possibilities, including features that assume future AFS development, and is not meant as a practical cell. Hosts afsdb1 and afsdb2 share priority 0 with weights 2 and 4 for UDP VLDB service. Host afsdb3 has priority 1 on the non-standard port 65500, so it is used only if the other two are unreachable.

Only afsdb1 provides UDP PTS service. The example also shows a hypothetical TCP version of the services on afsdb3; the RFC notes that no such TCP-based AFS protocol existed when it was written. A single AFSDB record lists only afsdb1, since only it offers both services over UDP on the standard ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a pretend address book for a pretend company. It shows a first-choice server, a backup server on an unusual door, and a single old-style entry for older machines.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SRV records pose the same risks as AFSDB. Unless DNS answers are checked for integrity and authenticity, an attacker can forge replies that point clients at a VLDB or PTS server the attacker controls. From there the attacker can mislead the client about volumes, file servers and file contents, and may be able to compromise the client further if it runs programs from the cell.

Authenticating the server prevents this, but much AFS access is unauthenticated, and clients may fall back to unauthenticated access after a failure. DNSSEC can prevent the DNS-based attack, but the underlying weakness is in the AFS protocol itself and could be exploited by forging VLDB query results. Adding SRV records does not make it worse; it only adds another equivalent point of attack.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster fakes the address book, you could knock on the wrong door. Checking the address book helps, but the real fix has to come from the shared-folder system itself.
